extracted.intended_audience: engineers, municipal planners, investors, and informed general readers interested in comparing electric and gas lighting (late 19th-century context)
extracted.subtask_description: Economic and technical comparison of electric (incandescent) and coal/water gas lighting systems, including plant sizing, per-mile mains costs, operating expenses, and assumptions (lamps per horsepower, coal consumption, depreciation, interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements entering into the cost of the light to the company
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements entering into the cost of the light to the company are, in each case, the interest on the investment, depreciation (amount spent each year in keeping the property in good condition), the labor of all kinds (manufacture, distribution, and management), and the cost of the materials used in its production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items constitute the company expense account (excluding taxes). When comparing systems, include interest, depreciation (both producing works and mains), labor (manufacture/distribution/management), and material costs. The text uses these as the baseline for per-1,000-feet comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depreciation of producing works (allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the four metropolitan gas companies depreciation was about 9.86 cents per 1,000 feet (about 5.5% on the producing portion). For the electric plant four per cent is a sufficient allowance for the same item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating yearly charges include a producing-works depreciation rate appropriate to the technology; the author uses ~5.5% for gas-producing plant and 4% for electric producing plant, converting to cents per 1,000 feet for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depreciation of mains (treatment and variability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depreciation of mains is exceedingly variable; for gas mains the author takes 2% of entire cost of the mains, while for electric mains depreciation is reckoned only upon their cost exclusive of copper (as copper is practically indestructible and reusable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mains depreciation separately from producing-works depreciation. For electric mains exclude copper from the depreciable base (reduced yearly charge). Use realistic local soil/installation conditions to adjust percentage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest on investment (include at prevailing rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest on the investment is the same in each case and amounts to $24,000 a year at four per cent, and to 12 cents per 1,000 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include interest expense (e.g., use a market rate like 4% in example) when converting plant investment to annual cost per unit of service (per 1,000 feet equivalent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing and distribution expenses (labor staffing and costing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing and distribution include purification, salaries, wages for carbonizing, wear and tear, and labor for inspection of meters, etc. Example figures: for gas manufacturing ~12 cents per 1,000 feet (English figures adjusted), distribution ~4.4 cents (rounded to 5 cents for American works), electric station staffing: one chief engineer $125/month, three assistants $75, five firemen $60 — total ~$15,600/year or 7.8 cents per 1,000 feet, plus electrician/incidentals to ~9 cents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing systems, itemize labor by function (manufacture, purification, inspection/meters, station staff) and convert monthly/yearly payrolls into unit costs. Deduct mains depreciation where already included in distribution charges for gas to avoid double-counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of coal (gas) net of residuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost of coal per 1,000 feet of gas made in London companies was ~36.76 cents offset by sale of residuals (coke, tar, ammonia) totaling 24.06 cents, leaving net cost ~12.8 cents. Using American coal prices (e.g., $4.50/ton and 10,000 feet per ton) yields 45 cents per 1,000 feet before residuals; under favorable residual recovery net cost could be ~22.5 cents per 1,000 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the sale/value of residuals when calculating net coal cost for gas. Use local coal prices and the gas yield per ton to compute per-unit coal cost; subtract expected residual receipts (which can vary widely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of fuel/power for electricity (coal per horsepower-hour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Edison's tests: able to maintain a horse-power an hour with five pounds of slack costing $2.45/ton; for conservative estimates a 200-horse engine consumption of four pounds of coal an hour at $4.50/ton is used. A horse-power then costs 4/2240 ton* $4.50 ≈ fractional cents per hour; maintenance for an hour of 200 electric burners (equivalent to 1,000 feet of gas) costs 20 cents (electric) versus 22.5 cents (gas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When valuing electricity-based lighting, convert engine/boiler fuel consumption into cost per horsepower-hour and then into cost per lamp or per 1,000-feet equivalent. Use conservative test/proven consumption figures but allow for likely improvements over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: lamps per horsepower (system sizing metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison assumes eight sixteen-candle lamps maintained throughout the system for each actual horse-power applied to the dynamo. Increasing lamps per horse-power (e.g., to ten) materially reduces plant and production cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and state a lamps-per-horsepower assumption explicitly; it strongly influences plant-capacity needs, conductor sizing, interest and depreciation per lamp, and the overall cost-per-unit of light. Consider sensitivity to improved lamp efficiency and lamp life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main/conductor costing per mile (materials, enclosure, laying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present conductors: half-round copper rods equivalent to 1/2-inch round rods weighing ~3986.4 lb/mi costing 28 cents/lb → $1,116 per mile; two rods → $2,232; plus $1,200/mi for wrought-iron tube, boxes, insulation and $1,000/mi for laying → total $4,432 per mile for ordinary mains. Feeders (¾-inch equivalent) cost more (~$7,196/mi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating distribution mains cost, compute metal weight × unit price, then add enclosure, insulating materials, joint boxes, and installation/laying costs per mile. Distinguish between main conductors and larger feeders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilers and engines cost assumptions for plant
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-hundred-horse engines can be obtained at ~$18 per horse-power ($3,600 each in author's estimate, though Edison states $1,750 delivered). Sectional/water-tube boilers cost ~$20 per horse-power (set ready for use including stack and coal-handling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include up-front capital costs of prime movers and boilers in plant investment. Use market quotes from large buyers and note potential discrepancies; small changes in unit price have modest effect on yearly plant account per 1,000 units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of copper as non-depreciable (reusable) in electric mains
rubrics_metrics.description: Copper in electric mains is practically indestructible and can be used again and again; depreciation of electric mains should be reckoned upon their cost exclusive of the copper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude recoverable materials (like copper) from the depreciable base when estimating annual depreciation for electric distribution mains; this reduces yearly charges and changes comparative economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal/replacement of lamps (who bears cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Renewal of incandescent lamps is an item which with general introduction would fall directly upon the consumer, but if charged to the supplying company, with lamps life of 600 hours costing 30 cents, the item amounts to 10 cents per 1,000 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clearly whether lamp replacement costs are borne by consumer or supplier. If included in company costs, convert lamp life and unit cost into per-unit service (per 1,000 feet or per lamp-hour) and include in manufacturing/operating expenses. Note technological improvements (longer life) will reduce this charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include rent, taxes, management, law charges, bad debts, and incidentals
rubrics_metrics.description: These cannot be separately arrived at closely but may be taken in the lump as about the same proportion of total charges as in London companies (16% exclusive of interest on investment). In the present case this equals ~9.4 cents per 1,000 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add an overhead lump-sum percentage (e.g., 16% of applicable charges) for rent/taxes/management/etc. to make the comparison more realistic; ensure consistency (exclude interest if specified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a common unit metric (per 1,000 feet equivalent) for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper converts all items to 'per 1,000 feet' (or the electric equivalent) to compare plant account, manufacturing expenses, and working expenses side by side (tables showing Interest, Depreciation, Manufacturing, Coal or Power, Distribution, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a single comparable unit (here 1,000 cubic feet of gas equivalent) and convert all capital and operating costs into that unit to produce an apples-to-apples comparison between technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider competitor technologies and future improvements (water-gas and burners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Water-gas (from steam decomposition) has advantages: less costly producing plant, smaller labor account, decreased depreciation; may produce a sixteen-candle gas costing ~28 cents materials and total not exceeding 60 cents. Improved gas burners (Siemens high-power) can more than double illumination from sixteen-candle gas; incandescent lamps' performance improvements also affect the comparative economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing systems, include plausible alternative manufacturing methods and distribution/burner improvements. Perform scenario analysis for technological change (both for electric lamps and gas manufacturing/burners) rather than assuming static technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant sizing, reserve capacity and station placement assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Example sizing: to cover three square miles two distributing stations suffice; steam-dynamos taken as 200 HP each, thirteen to one station and twelve to the other; reserve plant accounted for by engines that can be forced ~20% or run whole plant at normal rate. Reserve and station counts are used to size investment and calculate per-unit plant costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit assumptions about geographic coverage, number/size of stations, machine horsepower, and reserve margin (e.g., 20% forcing). These choices materially affect capital cost, mains mileage, and per-unit annual charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary comparison table structure (Plant, Manufacturing, Working expenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author structures the cost comparison into grouped accounts per 1,000 feet: Plant Account (Interest, Depreciation producing works, Depreciation mains), Manufacturing expenses (Labor, Coal/Power), Working expenses (Distribution), then totals and overheads to produce final cents per 1,000 feet for Gas and Electricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize comparative costs into consistent grouped accounts (plant, manufacturing, working/overhead) to make the differences transparent. Present subtotals and then add uniform overheads to reach total unit cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants of human longevity (essay criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longevity is influenced by material prosperity, the absence of misfortune, management of the individual, diet, climate, administrative conditions, good crops/industrial development, mental state (will to live, cheerfulness), occupation/hobbies, and social/political stability. The author cites evidence and anecdotes showing moral/psychological factors (success, hope, willpower) and physical/environmental factors both play large roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing longevity, account for both social/environmental determinants (diet, climate, governance, public health) and psychological/behavioral determinants (cheerfulness, purpose, resistance to despair). Use historical and anecdotal evidence cautiously; separate correlation from causation and acknowledge variability across regions and eras.
